name: contravariant-validators
intent: Make a check on a value a reusable first-class validator that can be adapted to other input types and combined with other validators, so that rules are composed out of parts instead of being re-implemented for every type that carries the same value.
problem: Reusable checks that narrow on a condition - 'is this a valid port', 'is this host name well formed', 'is this account allowed' - are needed for many representations of the same value (wire DTO, domain type, CLI string, database row). Written as a method or an inline if per site, the same rule is duplicated, cannot be combined with another rule without editing the check, and every new rule means editing the class that holds the data.
context: Value-level validation and parsing at a boundary: configuration and environment loading, request or message payload checking, domain-primitive construction, form validation, authorization predicates. It applies wherever checks are pure functions of one input, must be reused across several input shapes or composed into rule sets, and the language offers first-class functions or a typeclass layer for the composition. Rules that depend on I/O, transactions or clock state are outside the pattern.
benefits: Rules are values: a validator written for a core type is reused for every representation of that type through a projection (contramap), instead of one check class per carrier type.
New rules compose without touching the checked types or the existing rules (open/closed): divide/choose/and/or/refine build larger validators from smaller ones.

Independent failures can be reported together when the verdict carries a monoid: the same structure that makes a rule set composable makes 'all errors at once' a property of the composition rather than a special case.
Testability: each rule is a pure function of one value, and the composed rule set is exercised without a system under test, which is exactly the part that unit tests should cover.
Laws instead of convention: conquer/divide/contramap satisfy identity and associativity laws, so refactoring or reordering a rule set provably preserves meaning.
Narrowing at the boundary (parse, don't validate): the validator can produce a refined value, so inner code works with data that cannot be invalid and does not re-check.
tradeoffs: The combinator layer fixes how verdicts combine, not what a verdict is: the canonical instance is Predicate = input -> Bool, so a composed validator that rejects carries no reason, no field path and no rule identity until you invent a verdict type and an accumulation strategy.

Accumulation is easy to lose: switching the same rule set to a monadic pipeline (flatMap, for-comprehension, Result chaining) silently changes fail-fast semantics versus applicative divide, and the code still looks right.

choose needs the classify function (a -> Either b c) as its input: the hard judgement 'which branch is this?' must already exist and be total. Without a real sum type the branch knowledge gets duplicated inside the individual validators.

Fusing rules into one value hides which rule failed unless each carries a tag, hurts stepping through a debugger, and erases the sequence of checks; deeply fused point-free chains are hard to read and review.

Type erasure costs allocations and indirect calls (std::function, BoxPredicate, Box<dyn Fn>, delegate closures), while monomorphised templates, generics and function types cost nothing extra - the same pattern spans zero-overhead and per-item allocation depending on the realization.

Declarative realizations (Bean Validation, DataAnnotations, FluentValidation, pydantic, zod, validator) put rules next to the data and validate whole structures, but the same rule then tends to exist in schema, annotation and hand-written form, and nothing in the typeclass layer provides rule identity to prevent drift.

The pattern narrows values and does not replace decisions that need I/O or state (uniqueness, rate limits, aggregate invariants): those belong in the application service, and pretending otherwise produces validators that are neither pure nor reusable.

participants.responsibility: A value from the input type to a verdict - a predicate, a refined result, a rule object. It consumes its input; it never produces or owns it.
Adapts an existing validator to a new input type through a pure projection, so one rule serves every representation of the value (DTO, domain type, CLI string).
Splits the input into independent parts, runs one validator per part and combines the verdicts with the verdict monoid; conquer is the validator that accepts everything and acts as the identity.
Routes the input to one of two validators according to a case split, so branch-specific rules stay separate; lose is the validator for a branch that cannot occur.
Defines what a failure is (reason, path, rule id) and how two verdicts combine - conjunction for accept/reject predicates, error accumulation for user-facing validation.

Applies the composed validator once at the edge (config loader, request handler, parser), turns the verdict into an error report, and passes the narrowed value inward so inner layers do not re-validate.

use_cases: Configuration and environment loading: parse an untyped map into a typed configuration record, with one reusable validator per field and all field errors reported in one pass.

Request and message payload checking: compose a schema/rule set from reusable field validators plus cross-field rules, then dispatch branch-specific rules after a case split (choose) on the payload type.

Domain primitives and refinement: define positive/Email/Iban-style checks once and apply them to every representation of that value through projections, or carry them in the type system as refinement/branded types.
Authorization and feature predicates: composable rules over a request or principal (admin OR owner, enabled AND within quota), each rule written against a small projection of the context.
Form and API error reporting: collect every failed rule with its field path instead of failing at the first problem, by combining verdicts with an accumulating monoid.

Archival or search predicates: build a rule tree once (conjunction of filters over properties) and hand it to a framework that evaluates it later (Foundation Predicate, SwiftData/query engines, filter DSLs).
gRPC and protobuf boundaries: validate oneof/discriminated union payloads by routing each variant through its own validator using choose, while shared fields are validated once via divide.

Event-sourced aggregate validation: validate command payloads at the aggregate root, collecting every domain invariant violation before rejecting the command rather than failing on the first broken rule.

Multi-tenant SaaS rule sets: compose tenant-specific validators from shared base rules via divide/conquer, so the same field rules are reused across tenants with tenant-specific constraint values injected via contramap.

gRPC/protobuf and wire format boundaries: validate at the deserialization boundary before the parsed message reaches business logic, using a composed validator that is reused for CLI, test fixtures, and service-to-service calls.

Typed FP standard libraries shipping the combinators as an API: Arrow Kotlin exposes Contravariant/Divisible/Decidable type classes (conquer, divide, choose, lose) for carriers like Predicate and Serializer, and the contravariant package in Haskell instances them for Predicate, Comparison, Equivalence and Op - the pattern realized as library infrastructure rather than application code.

Refinement-type libraries as validator stores: fthomas/refined attaches type-level predicates (Positive, MatchesRegex, Uri) composed with And/Or/Not to values, with custom checks arriving as a Validate instance built by Validate.fromPredicate - the same rule set read at compile time by macros and at runtime by refineV.

Accumulating verdict monoids in production effect systems: ZIO Prelude's Validation[E, A] carries a NonEmptyChunk of errors and composes per-field checks with validateWith, so a registration form built from independent field validators reports every violation in one pass instead of one per round trip.
avoid_when: One or two checks on a single call site: an if-statement or a require assertion names the intent better and is easier to read.
Fail-fast semantics are required: Result/Either/exception short-circuiting is the simpler tool; validation that must report everything is a different (accumulating) combination.

The schema language you already use can express the rule (JSON Schema, OpenAPI, XML Schema, database constraints, OpenAPI-generated validators): the schema should stay the single source instead of being re-implemented as predicates.
The check needs I/O or shared state (uniqueness in the database, rate limits, external lookups): keep it in the application service and inject an already-computed answer into the pure rule.

The type system can carry the constraint (newtype plus smart constructor, refinement type, branded type): that removes the possibility of an invalid value rather than reporting it, which is stronger than any validator.
The check exists to satisfy a validator framework nobody else reads (an annotation with a hand-written predicate behind it) and the rule is used once: prefer the framework's own rules or plain code.
anti_patterns: One validator class (or interface implementation) per validated type: the OO re-invention of the pattern, which duplicates every rule per carrier type and needs a new class for each new input shape.

Boolean-blind validation: composing predicates that return only true/false and reconstructing the error message at the call site, so message and rule drift apart and multi-error reporting is impossible.
Short-circuit masquerading as validation: an Either/Result flatMap chain reported as 'validation' that shows the user one error per attempt.
Rules spread over three notations - schema, annotation and hand-written predicate - with no single composition point, so the same field is checked differently in different layers.
Over-applied point-free: a fused contramap/divide/choose expression nobody can read, step through or attach a rule id to.
Validating in every layer (controller, service, repository) with re-implemented rules, producing three failure dialects for the same data.
Validators with side effects (writing logs, mutating the input, caching) hidden behind a boolean signature, which makes the rule set order-dependent.
Shotgun parsing: spreading validation checks across processing code rather than at the boundary, hoping one of them catches invalid cases - the antithesis of parse, don't validate.
design_principles: Composition over inheritance: validators are values combined with contramap/divide/choose (or and/or/refine), not a Validator class hierarchy.
Open/closed principle: new rules arrive as new composed values; the validated types and existing rules stay untouched.
Single responsibility per rule: one concern per validator, composed into a rule set, so every failure maps to exactly one rule.
Lawful composition: identity (conquer) and associativity of divide/choose make rule sets refactorable without changing meaning.
Parse, don't validate: the boundary function returns a narrowed value, making the invariant impossible to forget downstream.
Dependency inversion on input shape: rules depend on the smallest projection they need, not on the whole object graph.
best_practices: Decide the verdict type first: a failure carries a reason, a path and ideally a rule id, and independent failures are combined with a monoid (ValidatedNel, Vec<Error>, issue list) rather than short-circuiting.
Write each rule against the smallest projection and assemble with divide/and; keep rules pure, deterministic and free of I/O.
Bind every intermediate composed validator to a name (val, const, let) so failures and stack traces point at something meaningful instead of an anonymous fused expression.
Make the classify function of choose explicit and total, and prefer a real sum type (sealed interface, enum, discriminated union, variant) over a boolean tag.
Apply the composed validator exactly once at the boundary and pass the narrowed result inward; do not re-validate in inner layers.
Test rules individually with table-driven cases and the composition with property-based tests over the laws (identity and associativity), not with one test per composed rule set.
Keep rule identity stable (ids, paths) so error reports, metrics and documentation can refer to a rule after it moves.
Place framework-level rules (annotations, schema) in the layer that owns the data shape and share the same rule implementations with hand-written predicates instead of duplicating them.
In TypeScript with Zod, prefer z.infer<typeof Schema> for type inference rather than manually maintaining a separate interface, to guarantee the runtime and compile-time types never drift apart.

Define base schemas for reusable fields (Email, UUID, pagination params) once in a shared schemas module and compose them into endpoint-specific schemas via .extend() or .merge(), so rule updates propagate automatically.
Use discriminated unions (z.discriminatedUnion, z.enum) for routing validators via choose rather than boolean tag values, to keep the classify function total and avoid missing branch coverage.
In Zod, use .superRefine() for cross-field checks only; for single-field rules prefer built-in validators (.min, .max, .regex) which compose better under .and() and participate in schema merging.

When async validation is required (e.g., database uniqueness checks), isolate it from pure validators and run it in a separate pipeline stage after all accumulating synchronous validations have passed - never mix async flatMap with an accumulating applicative validator.

For Rust, prefer the type-lib or refined_type crate's zero-sized marker types for validators, which avoids heap allocation and uses the type system to select rules rather than storing them at runtime.

In languages with a Validation type (Cats Validated, Scalaz Validation, Zio's Validation), always use the accumulating Applicative instance rather than Either-based validation when collecting all errors is the goal.

Use .pipe() or equivalent chaining in schema libraries (Zod's .pipe(), pydantic's model_validator) for multi-stage validation where the output of one stage is the input of the next, rather than nesting validators or relying on implicit ordering.

related_patterns_notes.functor: A contravariant functor is the categorical dual of a (covariant) functor: while a covariant functor maps the output type of a function forward (Fmap: (A => B) => F[A] => F[B]), a contravariant functor maps the input type backward (Contramap: (B => A) => F[A] => F[B]). A Validator is the canonical example: given a validator for A and a function B => A, you get a validator for B. Without contramap, each input shape would need its own rule implementation.
related_patterns_notes.applicative: Applicative composition lets multiple independent validators run on the same input and combine their results (divide/conquer). The applicative functor laws guarantee that the order of combination does not affect the outcome, which is what enables accumulating all errors rather than short-circuiting on the first. The Validator type is both contravariant (input goes backward) and applicative (independent results combine forward), making it a Profunctor.
related_patterns_notes.monad: Monadic bind (flatMap, >>=) produces fail-fast sequential validation where each step can influence which subsequent checks run. This is a valid design choice (e.g., parser combinators) but is a different pattern from the accumulative applicative style. Using monadic chaining when accumulation is intended is the 'short-circuit masquerading as validation' anti-pattern. The key distinction: monad = sequential dependent checks; applicative = independent parallel checks.
related_patterns_notes.specification: The Specification pattern (Evans) expresses business rules as composable objects with and/or/not combinators. Contravariant validators are the functional equivalent: a Validator IS a Specification (a predicate with a verdict), and divide/conquer/contramap are the categorical realization of and/or/not. The key addition is the contravariant structure (contramap) which makes specifications reusable across different input shapes in a way the original OO pattern does not provide.
related_patterns_notes.filterer: Filterer (P of E, a generalized Optional) extracts a predicate from a container and applies it to the contained value. Both Filterer and Validator are contravariant: Filterer contramaps over the predicate, Validator contramaps over its input. The Validator pattern can be seen as a Filterer where the 'container' is the boundary between unvalidated and validated data, and contramap models the act of adapting a rule to a new input shape.
related_patterns_notes.visitor: Visitor and Contravariant Validator both use a classify-then-dispatch pattern: Visitor uses double dispatch to route to the right handler based on the dynamic type of an argument; choose uses a total function (a => Either b c) to route to the right validator based on a discriminator. Both separate the 'which case' decision from the 'what to do in each case' logic, but Validator does it statically (at composition time) while Visitor does it dynamically (at runtime).
related_patterns_notes.newtype: A newtype (or opaque type, smart constructor) is the runtime enforcement complement to a contravariant validator: the newtype makes an illegal state unrepresentable by construction, while a validator proves the property at the boundary. The two compose: use a newtype wrapper (Username, PositiveInt, Email) that is constructed only from a validator's narrowed result, so a Username cannot exist without having passed the non-empty and valid-characters rules. The validator handles the parse step; the newtype enforces the invariant for the rest of the program.
